title: A tsunami crosses the deep ocean at over 800 km/h as a swell only about 30 cm high
body: A tsunami’s speed depends on the depth of the water, so over the deep ocean it can travel at **well over 800 km/h**. Out there its wavelength can be up to 200 km, and it usually lifts the sea surface by only about 300 mm, which makes it hard to detect. As it reaches shallower water near a coast it slows to below 80 km/h, and the water piles up into a wave that grows in height, a process called shoaling.

slides.alt: Animated world map: after the March 2011 earthquake off Japan, a ring of red and blue wave crests spreads out from Japan and fills the whole Pacific, reaching the Americas, Australia and Antarctica.
slides.caption: NOAA’s model of the tsunami from the magnitude 9.0 earthquake off Japan on 11 March 2011: in about a day of simulated time it fans out across the entire Pacific.

slides.heading: Tsunami speed
slides.note: It slows to below 80 km/h near shore; over deep water it travels at well over 800 km/h

left.label: Deep ocean
left.text: Well over 800 km/h, a wavelength of up to 200 km, and a swell of about 30 cm

right.label: Near the coast
right.text: Below 80 km/h, and growing taller as the water gets shallower

slides.prompt: Out in deep water, how long does one tsunami wave take to rise and fall at a single spot?
slides.detail: A tsunami usually arrives as a series of waves, and the gaps between them can range from minutes to hours.

slides.question: What sets how fast a tsunami travels across the open sea?
slides.explanation: Its speed comes from the depth: roughly the square root of gravity times the depth of the water, so it is fastest over the deepest ocean.
